title: Stanford's revised Canaries paper: young workers in AI-exposed jobs are now 19% behind their peers
subtitle: The August 2026 update to Brynjolfsson's employment study finds no economy-wide displacement — but the gap between 22–25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations and their less-exposed peers has widened again, driven by declines in software engineering and customer service.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Stanford Digital Economy Lab released the August 2026 revision of Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts About the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence, its long-running study of ADP payroll data since the launch of ChatGPT. The updated headline: employment among workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations is now roughly 19 percent below where it would sit if it had tracked the trajectory of similarly aged workers in less-exposed occupations. Employment in the two most-exposed quintiles fell about 11 percent between November 2022 and June 2026 for that age group; employment in the three least-exposed quintiles grew about 10 percent over the same span.

The mechanism is worth reading carefully. The paper — by Erik Brynjolfsson and co-authors — argues that AI substitutes most effectively for codified, formal knowledge, which is exactly what junior software engineers, entry-level customer-service agents, and other early-career knowledge workers spend their first years applying. Experienced workers in the same occupations, by contrast, deploy tacit knowledge acquired through mentorship and reps, which the current generation of models does not replicate well. That's why the pattern shows up as a widening age gap inside AI-exposed roles rather than as a mass layoff line item.

It also lands against a specific policy backdrop. The U.S. June jobs report, EU AI Act employment-impact reporting rules now in force, and this week's Stanford revision are all pointing at the same phenomenon from different angles — no headline unemployment shock, but a real reshaping of who gets hired at the entry level. The Canaries authors have been careful not to attribute the gap solely to AI; interest rates and post-pandemic hiring correction still explain a share of it. But the AI-exposure coefficient has strengthened, not weakened, across successive revisions.

Takeaway for learners: if you are early in your career in a codified-knowledge field, the practical response is to shift the balance of what you learn toward the tacit part of the work. Ship things, take on the messy end-to-end responsibilities most juniors dodge, work in-person with senior operators when you can, and build a portfolio of judgment calls you actually made. The Canaries data is not telling you the door is closed — it is telling you that the door labeled 'junior task-executor' is narrowing, while the door labeled 'apprentice who takes real responsibility' is not.
